title: Musadik Malik: Why Pakistan’s face of Indus waters advocacy is attending Delhi SCO meet
content_html:
Islamabad officially put Musadik Malik’s (L) name on Saturday — a day after Union Culture Minister Gajendra Shekhawat said he was “hopeful” of Pakistan’s presence at the event. Photo: Pakistan Senate/PIB
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

Pakistan is sending its Climate Change and Environmental Coordination Minister, Musadik Masood Malik, to New Delhi for the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum from November 20 to 22.

As per protocol, India had invited Pakistan’s Culture and National Heritage Minister, Aurangzeb Khan Khichi, for the forum. However, Pakistan decided to send Malik instead after a high-level discussion between Foreign Ministry officials in Islamabad and the High Commission in New Delhi on Saturday (November 14).

So, who is Malik, and why is Pakistan sending him instead of their Culture Minister for a civilisational dialogue? And what have been his recent statements on India in context of the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT), currently in abeyance? We explain.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Who is Musadik Masood Malik?

A senior member of the Pakistan Muslim League (Nawaz) and a sitting Senator, he assumed the climate portfolio in March 2025 under Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. He previously held the positions of Minister of Water and Power in the caretaker cabinet led by Mir Hazar Khan Khoso (March-June 2013) and the Minister for Water Resources and Minister of Energy (2022-23) in the earlier Sharif government. He was also the spokesperson for former Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif in 2014.

The invitation to Pakistan’s minister is part of New Delhi’s obligation to invite representatives from all SCO member countries, as it had proposed to host the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum. It is, however, the invited country’s prerogative to decide on its representation, so Islamabad officially put Malik’s name on Saturday — a day after Union Culture Minister Gajendra Shekhawat said he was “hopeful” of Pakistan’s presence at the event.

Announcing the decision to attend the summit, Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry said, “The event will bring together representatives from SCO member states to exchange views on issues related to civilisational dialogue and cultural understanding.”

Also in Explained | Expert Explains | Why does SCO matter to India? It’s not just soft power

While Malik is expected to spend two days in New Delhi, the final itinerary is still being worked out in discussion with the Pakistan High Commission in New Delhi. Malik has just returned after attending the COP31 UN climate conference in Turkey, and the details of his possible meetings with the Indian side — if any — are being discussed. 

Story continues below this ad

This is the first such invitation to a senior Pakistan minister since India and Pakistan had a military confrontation in May 2025, where India conducted its response to the Pahalgam terror attack (in April 2025) under Operation Sindoor.

With Malik attending the meet, it will be a first for a Pakistani minister since May 2023, when India had hosted then Foreign Minister Bilawal Bhutto Zardari in Goa for the SCO Foreign Ministers’ meeting.

What did Musadik Malik say about the Indus Waters Treaty?

Pakistan has been repeatedly raising the issue of India putting the IWT in abeyance. While Malik doesn’t handle the issue directly and is handled by the Water Resources ministry, he has been the public face for international advocacy on it.

Story continues below this ad

In June this year, Malik — a technocrat turned minister — said in a press conference that Pakistan would “cut off those hands” that are attempting to control the Indus waters. He recently said that Pakistan is taking the IWT issue beyond bilateral discussions to the United Nations and other international arbitration forums, calling it “a question of justice and downstream rights”.

Explained F

When asked by Pakistani media whether he would raise India’s decision to place the Treaty in abeyance during his address in New Delhi, Malik said the trip is not a bilateral negotiation. He, however, declined to rule out raising the issue.

How is Pakistan asserting its claim on the Indus?

In recent months, Pakistan has been asserting its claim on the Indus by highlighting the Indus Valley civilisation of Mohenjodaro, Harappa, and other ancient sites in the country.

Story continues below this ad

On World Heritage Day (April 18) this year, Pakistani PM Shehbaz Sharif had referred to the Indus Valley civilisation in his remarks, saying, “Pakistan’s cultural heritage is enriched with a multifaceted civilisation. Our homeland carries the legacy of some of the world’s oldest civilisations, reflecting a vibrant tapestry of human creativity and diversity.”

When asked about this last week, Shekhawat said, “When a country tries to talk about 5,000 years of Indus Valley Civilisation, they should be self-aware that they didn’t exist at the time. Their story is just 80 years old.”

title: How Indira Gandhi turned the sari into a powerful political statement
content_html:
Former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi at the Carlyle Hotel, New York City, March 31 1966. (Wikimedia Commons)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

The year was 1978. After crucial victories in the Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka Assembly elections in February, Indira Gandhi’s next fight was a Lok Sabha by-election in her home state of Uttar Pradesh—Azamgarh.

Gandhi handpicked her party’s candidate: Mohsina Kidwai, a Muslim woman who belonged to one of Uttar Pradesh’s old Congress families. In Indira Gandhi: A Biography (1995), Pupul Jayakar wrote, “On her behalf Indira, dressed in a handspun cotton sari with a coarse long-sleeved blouse, her head modestly covered, fought a relentless campaign.”

In the campaign’s final phase, with Kidwai by her side, Gandhi addressed 24 meetings in less than 30 hours. Along the way, she stopped to speak to groups of peasants, women and members of minority communities. “Though illiterate, the peasants of India through the centuries had gathered a wisdom through listening deeply and through direct and close observation. For them it was a wondrous thing that after fourteen hours on the road, travelling through dust and heat, Indira’s sari remained unwrinkled,” wrote Jayakar.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

What might appear trivial to the urban Indian could be deeply significant to the villager. “She would arrive to address them, her head covered; her fragility and the feeling of empathy that glowed from her, touched them.”

We take a closer look at how Gandhi turned the humble sari into an instrument of political mobilisation and spectacle.

The Nivi style of draping

Former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi holding an album of the commemorative stamps to release in honour of Jallianwala Bagh Martyrs. (Express Archive, 1969)

In The Sari (2008), Mukulika Banerjee and Daniel Miller observed: “Just as Mahatma Gandhi had spent years trying to find the right ‘look’ for a leader of a poor country bonded in political and economic oppression, so Indira Gandhi adroitly positioned herself in the status of Mother India, recognisable and familiar, yet transcendent and perfect.”

The drape she favoured was known as the Nivi. It emerged in the nineteenth century, arguably by Jnanadanandini Devi, the wife of Satyendranath Tagore. In the following decades, it gained popularity among women entering public life, including those participating in the platforms, protests and demonstrations of the anti-colonial movement. Their images, widely circulated in newspaper and magazine coverage of their political activities, helped popularise the style. “The Nivi style also featured in iconic nationalist propaganda images, such as the sari unfurled as the map of Mother India, by Raja Ravi Verma,” Banerjee and Miller noted.

Story continues below this ad
Also in Explained | The story of Saraiki, the language of viral folk song ‘Chhalrey Chhalrey Waal’

After Independence, the sari received a further boost from government information posters, film stars, politicians and Indian ambassadors. It was made the official uniform in the army, police and national airline.

Gradually, alternative regional draping styles began to recede from public view or remained confined to domestic spaces. The result, according to Banerjee and Miller, was a growing consciousness that what women wore was no longer simply a traditional, locally draped garment but the Sari—a recognisable national symbol.

“This association was cemented when, under the guidance of that consummate politician, Mrs Gandhi, the sari for a while became central to the construction of a visual image of India both internally and abroad,” they wrote.

 How Indira Gandhi made the sari her political signature

Former US President Reagan and Nancy Reagan with Prime Minister Indira Gandhi of India on the North Portico before a state dinner in July 1982 (Wikimedia Commons)

Jayakar’s account of Gandhi’s first visit to the United States in 1966 offers insight into the care she took over her appearance abroad. As meticulous about her wardrobe as she was about her speeches, Gandhi planned her attire down to the smallest detail. “Her sari, her blouse, her shoes, her bag were selected for every single function.” She even wrote to friends in the US seeking the latest cosmetics to conceal the shadows under her eyes and make her nose appear less prominent, Jayakar wrote.

Story continues below this ad

This attention to her appearance became particularly significant during her subsequent visits to the US in the 1970s, when the sari was increasingly associated with India’s national identity. Against the backdrop of the Cold War and India’s close economic and diplomatic ties with the Soviet Union, her public image carried considerable diplomatic significance. “For the American audience, she coiffured her hair with its distinctive streaks of white, and wore lipstick to complement the silk saris she had chosen, which were far more luxurious and colourful than her usual handlooms,” Banerjee and Miller wrote.

Also Read | Why a Japanese animated Ramayana faced opposition in India, but found an audience decades later

Back home, however, her saris were invariably handloom cotton, evoking the swadeshi and khadi movements championed by her father, Jawaharlal Nehru, and Mahatma Gandhi. According to Banerjee and Miller, “Indira wanted to look like an ordinary Indian woman, but as the quintessence of such womanhood, not merely an instance of it.”

As Nehru’s heir, she was conscious of her exceptional place in the popular imagination. Her challenge was to strike a delicate balance: to appear familiar and accessible to the masses while retaining the mystique that set her apart and inspired reverence. In this, she arguably succeeded. Women still recall the apparent effortlessness with which she wore saris.

“In public she never fidgeted, touching the pallu only to pull it over her head or hitching it up if the hot sun or muddy lanes demanded it. She moved in a fluid way that made you believe she was totally at home in a sari,” the authors wrote. For many middle-class women, Indira Gandhi thus became a style icon: a modern, professional woman who embraced traditional Indian attire.

Story continues below this ad

Another hallmark of her public appearances across the country was her choice of a sari made in the region she was visiting: a Tangail in Bengal, Coimbatore cotton in the south, or the distinctive Sanganer prints in the western states. “The sari conveyed a vivid message,” Banerjee and Miller observed, adding that it signalled “solidarity with the region”. Seeing the Prime Minister of India dressed in a regional weave gave local traditions national legitimacy.

The authors conclude: “If the nationalist movement determined a new pan-Indian style of wearing the sari, Mrs Gandhi set the trend for their enthusiastic acquisition.”

 How Indira Gandhi used the sari to shape India’s global image

Indira Gandhi acquired considerable diplomatic experience travelling with her father, in the capacity of de facto ‘First Lady’. Later, as Prime Minister, she was equally meticulous about hosting foreign dignitaries at home.

The careful following of protocol was visible in the numerous state visits Gandhi hosted and made as Prime Minister herself,” Smriti Sawkar wrote in her journal article Champion of the Third World: Indira Gandhi and the spectacle of the 1983 NAM Visit (2022).

Story continues below this ad

Her principal secretary in the 1980s, PC Alexander, recalled her close supervision of even the finer details of state hospitality, from selecting banquet menus to overseeing seating arrangements to ensure a smooth flow of conversation among guests.

An equally important consideration was her choice of clothing. Indira Gandhi meticulously calibrated her appearance to suit different settings.

Gandhi’s information adviser, B G Verghese, recalled: “At home she wore simple cotton or khadi saris with no more than a dark-beaded necklace, and kept her head covered. On state occasions, and especially when traveling abroad, she would dig into her rich wardrobe and appear elegantly attired, wearing high heels, her face lightly made up, and hair smartly styled…”

“Like her father who popularised the north-Indian achkan during his public appearances, Gandhi was also a champion of the traditional Indian sari,” Sawkar wrote.

title: How 2 major summits this week point to balance & bargain strategy in big-power diplomacy
content_html:
The meeting in China this week would be the first of its kind, with Presidents Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin. (Wikimedia Commons)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

Next week’s two summits are unlikely to set the world on fire. On Tuesday (November 17), the Quad leaders of Australia, India, Japan and the United States meet in Manila. On Thursday (November 19), Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping meet in Shenzhen. Taken together, they illuminate the rapidly changing nature of great-power politics: every major power is balancing and bargaining at the same time — simultaneously building coalitions, hedging against volatile partners and negotiating with adversaries.

This is not a world for the faint-hearted or those seeking ideological clarity. It rewards leaders who can navigate international contradictions and manage them to strengthen national capabilities.

Tuesday’s meeting in Manila of the leaders of Australia, India, Japan and the United States promises to resurrect a forum widely presumed dead. Thursday’s meeting in Shenzhen between Trump, Putin and Xi could give birth to a new format for consultations among the world’s three leading powers.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

The Quad’s agenda

The sequence is accidental but significant. Trump will meet America’s Asian partners before engaging the Chinese and Russian leaders. His preference might have been to focus on the latter, but the American establishment sees value in reassuring its allies. It also recognises that the Quad could strengthen Trump’s bargaining position with Xi and Putin.

Until recently, many had written off the Quad. The obituaries were premature. Ministerial consultations and practical cooperation continued despite the absence of summit-level engagement. Manila has an interesting place in the Quad’s history. The forum first met there in 2007. After becoming moribund, it was revived in Manila in 2017. Nearly a decade later, Manila is once again the setting for its renewal.

People gather near an installation promoting the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) China 2026 summit, in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 11. Leaders of the US, China and Russia will meet on its sidelines. (AP Photo/Ng Han Guan)

The proposed agenda is practical: critical minerals, resilient supply chains, energy security and the protection of commercial shipping. Maritime security, emerging technologies and strategic infrastructure remain important areas of cooperation.

Why G-3 is not quite a new Yalta

If Manila is renewing an established forum, Shenzhen is about launching a new one. The prospect of the American, Russian and Chinese presidents sitting together has revived speculation about a “new Yalta”, recalling the 1945 meeting of American, British and Soviet leaders that helped shape the post-war European order.

Story continues below this ad

But the historical analogy has limits. Yalta followed intensive cooperation among the Allies in defeating Nazi Germany. Trump, Putin and Xi are meeting amid expanding rivalry, with little agreement on the rules of the international order. Their immediate objective is to explore common ground rather than negotiate a grand geopolitical bargain.

Unsurprisingly, there is little clarity about the G-3 agenda. Nuclear arms control and cooperation in managing conflicts involving Iran and Ukraine are among the possibilities. Regulating artificial intelligence could be another. For Trump, the meeting reflects his faith in personal diplomacy and his ability to strike grand bargains. But much of the American foreign policy establishment remains sceptical of his approach to Putin and Xi. Any major concession by Trump to Russia and China with produce a vigorous American backlash.

Explained | The last US-Russia nuclear pact ends today. Is this the beginning of a new arms race?

For Putin, Shenzhen offers recognition of Russia’s enduring place at the global high table. Xi’s priorities are different. For Xi, trade, technology and strategic competition with Washington matter more than creating a trilateral institution. Yet Xi has little reason to reject a meeting that pleases Putin while consolidating Beijing’s status as the critical element of a global “triumvirate”.

The relevance for India 

For India, the Quad’s revival offers an opportunity to reboot its troubled relations with Washington. But as part of the hedge against American unpredictability, Delhi will continue to deepen cooperation with Europe, Russia and Japan while seeking to manage the structural tensions with China.

Story continues below this ad
China This Week | Spotlight on Chinese spying in Jensen Huang saga, and a Xi-Trump-Putin meeting

Critics at home and abroad have often derided India’s foreign policy as excessively transactional, especially its attempt to ride several horses, including BRICS and the Quad. But the new reality is that the great powers are doing much the same— balancing and bargaining. That is now baked into the international dynamic today.

Russia is a vociferous critic of America, but it seeks accommodation with Trump. China wants to reduce American influence in Asia but also seeks recognition as Washington’s equal. Neither sees a contradiction in pursuing apparently competing objectives.

For India, strategic flexibility can’t be an end in itself. An open-ended foreign policy, strong international partnerships must go hand in hand with the purposeful modernisation and upgradation of national capabilities. Without domestic unity and strength, India’s multi-alignment runs the risk of remaining trapped in intellectual abstraction rather than becoming a transformative tool towards advancing national interest.

(C. Raja Mohan is a contributing editor on International affairs for the Indian Express. He is professor and director at the Motwani-Jadeja Institute of American Studies, Jindal Global University, Delhi).

Tuesday’s meeting in Manila of the leaders of Australia, India, Japan and the United States promises to resurrect a forum widely presumed dead. Thursday’s meeting in Shenzhen between Trump, Putin and Xi could give birth to a new format for consultations among the world’s three leading powers.
Story continues below.

The Quad’s agenda
The sequence is accidental but significant. Trump will meet America’s Asian partners before engaging the Chinese and Russian leaders. His preference might have been to focus on the latter, but the American establishment sees value in reassuring its allies. It also recognises that the Quad could strengthen Trump’s bargaining position with Xi and Putin.
Until recently, many had written off the Quad. The obituaries were premature. Ministerial consultations and practical cooperation continued despite the absence of summit-level engagement. Manila has an interesting place in the Quad’s history. The forum first met there in 2007. After becoming moribund, it was revived in Manila in 2017. Nearly a decade later, Manila is once again the setting for its renewal.
People gather near an installation promoting the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) China 2026 summit, in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 11. Leaders of the US, China and Russia will meet on its sidelines. (AP Photo/Ng Han Guan)
The proposed agenda is practical: critical minerals, resilient supply chains, energy security and the protection of commercial shipping. Maritime security, emerging technologies and strategic infrastructure remain important areas of cooperation.
Why G-3 is not quite a new Yalta
If Manila is renewing an established forum, Shenzhen is about launching a new one. The prospect of the American, Russian and Chinese presidents sitting together has revived speculation about a “new Yalta”, recalling the 1945 meeting of American, British and Soviet leaders that helped shape the post-war European order.
Story continues below this ad
But the historical analogy has limits. Yalta followed intensive cooperation among the Allies in defeating Nazi Germany. Trump, Putin and Xi are meeting amid expanding rivalry, with little agreement on the rules of the international order. Their immediate objective is to explore common ground rather than negotiate a grand geopolitical bargain.
Unsurprisingly, there is little clarity about the G-3 agenda. Nuclear arms control and cooperation in managing conflicts involving Iran and Ukraine are among the possibilities. Regulating artificial intelligence could be another. For Trump, the meeting reflects his faith in personal diplomacy and his ability to strike grand bargains. But much of the American foreign policy establishment remains sceptical of his approach to Putin and Xi. Any major concession by Trump to Russia and China with produce a vigorous American backlash.
Explained
|
The last US-Russia nuclear pact ends today. Is this the beginning of a new arms race?
For Putin, Shenzhen offers recognition of Russia’s enduring place at the global high table. Xi’s priorities are different. For Xi, trade, technology and strategic competition with Washington matter more than creating a trilateral institution. Yet Xi has little reason to reject a meeting that pleases Putin while consolidating Beijing’s status as the critical element of a global “triumvirate”.
The relevance for India
For India, the Quad’s revival offers an opportunity to reboot its troubled relations with Washington. But as part of the hedge against American unpredictability, Delhi will continue to deepen cooperation with Europe, Russia and Japan while seeking to manage the structural tensions with China.
Story continues below this ad
China This Week
|
Spotlight on Chinese spying in Jensen Huang saga, and a Xi-Trump-Putin meeting
Critics at home and abroad have often derided India’s foreign policy as excessively transactional, especially its attempt to ride several horses, including BRICS and the Quad. But the new reality is that the great powers are doing much the same— balancing and bargaining. That is now baked into the international dynamic today.
Russia is a vociferous critic of America, but it seeks accommodation with Trump. China wants to reduce American influence in Asia but also seeks recognition as Washington’s equal. Neither sees a contradiction in pursuing apparently competing objectives.
For India, strategic flexibility can’t be an end in itself. An open-ended foreign policy, strong international partnerships must go hand in hand with the purposeful modernisation and upgradation of national capabilities. Without domestic unity and strength, India’s multi-alignment runs the risk of remaining trapped in intellectual abstraction rather than becoming a transformative tool towards advancing national interest.

title: Who keeps the internet running, and what happens when they can no longer afford to? An expert explains
content_html:
After the PHP2Shell flaws were disclosed, open-source maintainers helped get security fixes to users, including those on older PHP releases. (Magnific)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

When two critical security flaws in PHP, a programming language used by millions of websites, prompted organisations around the world to take services offline in October, Czech software engineer Ondřej Surý was among the maintainers who helped get the fixes to users.

The flaws, collectively dubbed PHP2Shell, led to precautionary shutdowns on October 21 of services run by Japan’s Finance Ministry, US human-resources platform BambooHR, the Port of Rotterdam in the Netherlands, and the Wikimedia Foundation, which operates Wikipedia.

Surý maintains widely used PHP software packages for Debian and Ubuntu, two Linux-based operating systems. He made patched versions available even for older releases of PHP that no longer receive official security updates.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Surý does much of this maintenance alongside his full-time job as Director of DNS Engineering at the Internet Systems Consortium (ISC), which develops software that helps translate website addresses into the numerical addresses computers use to communicate over the internet. He told The Indian Express that ISC had seen a sharp spike in vulnerability reports this year, although relatively few were serious. As AI tools make it easier to identify potential security flaws, assessing and fixing them still requires human expertise.

The experience raises a larger question about the sustainability of open-source software, whose underlying code is freely available for others to use, modify and distribute, and on which much of the internet depends. In an interview with The Indian Express, Surý discusses the PHP2Shell incident, the growing demands of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery, and why he believes businesses that profit from open-source software must help fund its maintenance. Edited excerpts:

Why does PHP matter to the functioning of the internet, and what made the recent PHP2Shell vulnerabilities particularly serious?

PHP is a programming language mainly used to develop websites. Roughly 70% of the web is powered by PHP. The recently discovered vulnerabilities in PHP were in the most serious category, remote code execution (RCE). In short, an attacker can exploit such a vulnerability to execute a program of their own choosing on a remote machine, potentially gaining full access to the server (the computer running the website or service).

When researchers discover a serious security flaw in widely used software, what happens next? Who develops the fix, who ensures it reaches users, and which parts of this process still depend heavily on human work?

Story continues below this ad

When ethical security researchers discover a serious security flaw, they contact the affected project or organisation privately. Any project or organisation that cares about security should have a mechanism through which researchers can report flaws in its software.

Also in Explained | What is PHP2Shell, and why did it force websites around the world offline?

Fixing the vulnerability is usually no different from fixing any other defect in the software, but the process depends on the size of the project. The work could fall to a single person in a small project or a handful of people in a larger one. They might or might not be employed to do this work.

In the case of PHP, there are a handful of volunteers for whom this is a side project, and very few people are employed directly by the PHP Foundation. Most of the important work still depends on people. As for when and how AI is used, it is important to remember that AI is just a tool that might or might not be useful in specific cases.

How did the early disclosure of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities affect the release of security updates?

Story continues below this ad

That was unfortunate because people who knew the original release schedule had made plans to properly release the software so that users could upgrade. The premature disclosure accelerated the whole process by a day.

Now, this is the bad part about AI: once details of the upcoming vulnerabilities were known, people started using AI to search for possible security flaws. It was no longer safe to stick to the original schedule because AI, as a tool, is quite good at finding security vulnerabilities, especially when guided by a skilled person.

AI tools are increasingly being used to discover vulnerabilities in software. Have you noticed any change in the number or complexity of vulnerability reports you receive, or in the work required to respond to them?

In my day job, I am the Director of DNS Engineering at ISC, responsible for BIND 9, a widely used open-source DNS server. There was a sharp spike this year in the frequency and depth of the vulnerability reports we received.

Story continues below this ad

Fortunately, after the initial surge, things went back to normal. We still receive occasional security reports, but only very few of them are serious enough to be handled as security vulnerabilities.

That is the thing with AI: it needs to be guided by an expert with domain knowledge. Otherwise, you often end up with serious-sounding reports about ordinary software bugs, or issues that are not even bugs.

Could AI also help maintainers identify security vulnerabilities themselves?

Not only that, maintainers can also use frontier AI models to find security vulnerabilities themselves. That said, both offensive (finding and exploiting vulnerabilities) and defensive (finding and fixing vulnerabilities) uses of AI need to be supervised by an expert. Otherwise, you might end up with a pile of mediocre-quality reports or, worse, AI might miss something serious.

You’ve spoken about the difficulty of sustaining open-source maintenance. Why does so much essential software depend on the work of relatively few people, and what would it take to support them adequately?

Story continues below this ad

When I joined university in 1995, free software was still very new, at least to me, and I found a purpose in making the fruits of my work freely available to others. It was a paradigm change, and I believe many people involved in the free-software movement are still driven by those ideals.

Black October | An expert explains how AI is changing cybersecurity

On the other hand, some people have built multibillion-dollar enterprises on top of open-source software and never even thought about supporting the software that allowed them to make money.

I think we need to find a balance. The free-software model is viable because it gives me and other developers freedom. On the other hand, if many people depend on that software for their livelihoods, we need a sustainable model that allows maintainers to continue working on the software they love without becoming exploited and exhausted.

Who should be responsible for funding the maintenance of open-source software?

Story continues below this ad

That question can easily be turned around: if the people maintaining the open-source software your company uses were to simply walk away, how large would your losses be in the event of a serious security vulnerability like the recent one in PHP? This should give people running businesses the answer to who should fund the work.

Not every open-source project has an organisation, whether for-profit or non-profit, behind it, but some do.

For instance, Software in the Public Interest is a non-profit organisation that provides financial and administrative support to projects such as Debian. Smaller projects can raise funds through platforms such as Open Collective, while PHP development receives funding through the PHP Foundation.

My PHP packaging work can be supported through Freexian’s PHP Long Term Support (PHP LTS) project, which provides maintenance and security updates for older PHP releases, or through GitHub Sponsors, which allows individuals and organisations to fund developers directly.

Story continues below this ad

At my day job, the Internet Systems Consortium (ISC) offers paid professional support for open-source projects such as BIND 9 and Kea, among other projects I am closely associated with.

title: ‘Very wrong signal to investors’: Behind Vedanta’s Anil Agarwal’s message to govt on ONGC transfer
content_html:
Water jets are sprayed on the rig during containment operations after a gas leakage was reported at an ONGC well near NH-216 in Geddada village (ANI Video Grab)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

Industrialist and chairman of the Vedanta group on Tuesday (November 17) cautioned that the Centre’s move to transfer operations of one of its oil and gas blocks to public sector major Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC) could send a “very wrong signal” to investors at a time when the government is looking to boost private and foreign investment in India’s hydrocarbon exploration and production sector. He also urged the government to maintain regulatory stability.

Behind Agarwal’s comments, which he made through a post on LinkedIn, is a hydrocarbon block that the government asked ONGC to take over, and the ongoing legal dispute around it.

The block Agarwal was referring to is the offshore Cambay basin oil and gas block CB-OS-02, which is off the Gujarat coast. Vedanta held a 40% participating interest in the block, and was its operator as well. ONGC held 50% in it and Invenire Petrodyne held the remaining 10%. But ONGC has now taken over the block, after the government refused to extend Vedanta’s application for an extension of its production sharing contract (PSC), and the Delhi High Court upheld that decision.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

The block in question and the story so far

The production sharing contract for the block expired on June 29, 2023, although Vedanta and its joint venture partners had applied for an extension on June 28, 2021, under the government’s 2017 PSC extension policy. The government, however, rejected Vedanta’s request in September last year and ordered the block to be handed over to ONGC.

Within days, Vedanta moved the Delhi High Court against the government’s decision. But on July 22 this year, its writ petition was dismissed by a single-judge bench of the court, which removed the interim stay that had earlier maintained status quo on the matter. Although Vedanta has appealed against the order before a division bench of the Delhi High Court, ONGC took control of the block and applied for a petroleum lease on July 28.

“Company (ONGC) has taken effective control of the said block with effect from July 22, 2026, consequent to Government’s directive to take control of the block. On July 22, 2026 Vedanta Limited has challenged the said order in Divisional Bench of the Hon’ble High Court of Delhi, and the matter is currently under adjudication.

The ultimate outcome of the litigation and its consequential impact, if any, cannot presently be determined,” ONGC said in a recent regulatory filing.

Story continues below this ad

“…subsequent to decision of Single Bench of Delhi High Court, ONGC has taken over the Block. The company (Vedanta Oil and Gas) has filed an appeal against the said dismissal before the Division Bench of the Delhi High Court. The hearings have concluded on 1st October and the matter is reserved for judgement,” Vedanta Oil and Gas said in a regulatory filing.

It added that in view of the developments, absence of a valid PSC, and the resulting uncertainty regarding recoverability of assets and receivables relating to the block, it has recognised an impairment charge of about Rs 379 crore during the first quarter of the current financial year. Vedanta also stopped recognising revenue and related expenses from the block from July 22.

Anil Agarwal’s objections

“Recently, our running field has been given to ONGC which will send a very wrong signal to investors. We are seeing such great energy and enthusiasm from global investors.

This is the time to keep the policy hand steady and not disrupt any existing operator. That shall go a long way in building and boosting global investor confidence. Let us all together make a determined move to increase domestic production and reduce oil and gas imports drastically,” Agarwal said in his LinkedIn post.

Story continues below this ad

“India is on the verge of something big in oil and gas. Like Guayana was ten years ago. We have a world-class policy ecosystem and a willingness to move from approvals to self-certification. Vedanta Oil and Gas, India’s largest private sector producer is committing USD 5 billion in investments to scale up production to 300,000-500,000 barrels per day. We have already moved into the deep sea Samudra Manthan programme,” he said.

Also Read | E20 petrol row: Why Karnataka’s allegations could reignite the ethanol blending debate

The timing of the developments pertaining to the CB-OS-02 block and Agarwal’s comments are significant as they come amid the government’s push to increase participation from the private sector and global oil and gas firms in India’s upstream oil and gas sector. India is the world’s third-largest consumer of crude oil and depends on imports to meet over 88% of its requirement. It is also a major importer of liquefied natural gas (LNG) with an import dependency of about 50%.

A series of oil and gas block auctions have been held over the years, but the interest from global investors has been largely absent. Among domestic private sector investors, Vedanta has been the biggest in terms of bidding for new blocks, and the auctions have largely seen participation from public sector oil and gas companies.

The Samudra Manthan scheme, or the National Offshore Exploration Scheme, which Agarwal referred to is an ambitious Rs 84,084-crore programme that the green-lighted about three-and-a-half months ago.

Story continues below this ad

The scheme will provide financial support for exploratory drilling in deep-sea and ultra-deep-sea areas and support building of common infrastructure for production of discovered hydrocarbons in offshore areas, apart from funding offshore data acquisition and developing hydrocarbon manufacturing and services zones. The Rs 84,084-crore outlay is for implementation till financial year 2030-31.

The Centre expects the Samudra Manthan scheme to catalyse reserve accretion of over 600 million tonnes of oil and oil equivalent gas (mtoe), while stimulating significant investments across the oil and gas exploration and production value chain.

The scheme will provide support of up to 50% of drilling cost or Rs 675 crore, whichever is lower, for every well drilled in deep-sea and ultra-deep-sea areas. Drilling at such depths is an expensive proposition, costing between $100 million and $250 million per well, as per industry estimates.

It is also risky as the drilling activity may not lead to any oil or natural gas discovery. In certain cases, even if hydrocarbons are discovered, it may not be commercially viable to exploit them. The scheme, officials expect, will mitigate some of the investment risks for upstream oil and gas players, and increase investment into the sector.

title: Why US is tightening AI chip restrictions amid the Nvidia-China controversy
content_html:
The Donald Trump administration has announced sweeping new restrictions aimed at preventing Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) companies from accessing advanced American chips through data centres located outside China, as Washington faces growing questions over the effectiveness of its technology export controls.

The new regulations, announced by the US Commerce Department on Monday (November 16), seek to close a significant loophole in America’s restrictions on advanced AI chips. While Washington has largely restricted the direct shipment of its most powerful processors to China, Chinese companies have been able to access the same computing capabilities by renting servers in countries such as Malaysia and Singapore.

The move comes amid a widening controversy surrounding chipmaker Nvidia, following the resignation of its chief executive Jensen Huang over revelations of his relationship with a woman suspected by US authorities of having links to Chinese intelligence. The woman, Alice Huang, was previously associated with Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, an Nvidia partner under investigation over possible violations of US chip export controls.

The restrictions also come as fresh research has raised questions over whether China’s leading AI developers, including DeepSeek and Moonshot AI, have already gained access to Nvidia’s export-restricted Blackwell chips.

New restrictions target overseas data centres and remote computing

Under the new interim final rule, issued by the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), overseas data centres that provide significant computing capacity to companies headquartered in China and other countries of concern will require US government authorisation to receive certain advanced American chips.

Importantly, the restrictions also cover companies whose ultimate parent organisation is based in these countries, seeking to prevent Chinese entities from circumventing the rules through subsidiaries registered elsewhere.

The rule sets a threshold of more than 12 million aggregate Total Processing Performance (TPP), a measure of computing capability, for restricted remote access. It also covers computing capacity distributed across interconnected data centres.

Separately, Washington has introduced additional licensing requirements for exports of advanced semiconductors to five countries — Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil — which it identifies as presenting a higher risk of chip diversion. Certain shipments to US-headquartered companies are exempt, subject to reporting requirements.

Existing data centres providing restricted computing services will have 90 days from the rule’s effective date to obtain the necessary licences to continue doing so. The regulations exempt commercial recommendation systems, including those used by e-commerce and social media companies.

The rule also formally rescinds the Biden administration’s broader AI Diffusion Rule, which was never enforced, replacing it with more targeted restrictions.

Washington’s concerns extend beyond the physical movement of chips

For several years, the US has sought to limit China’s access to advanced semiconductors, arguing that the same powerful processors used to develop commercial AI applications could also strengthen Beijing’s military and intelligence capabilities.

These chips are critical to training increasingly sophisticated AI models, and Washington has sought to preserve America’s technological advantage by restricting China’s access to the most advanced hardware.

Also Read | Jensen Huang resigns: Why his exit from Nvidia will be a test for the AI boom

However, restrictions on the physical shipment of processors have created another challenge for US authorities. Chinese companies can potentially access powerful American chips without importing them, simply by purchasing computing services from overseas data centres.

The Commerce Department said the new controls were necessary because advanced AI systems could be used to develop sophisticated weapons, conduct cyber-espionage, disrupt critical systems and support military operations.

Nvidia’s Megaspeed controversy has intensified scrutiny

The announcement comes against the backdrop of growing scrutiny of Nvidia and the Commerce Department over their handling of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based provider of computing services with operations linked to Southeast Asia.

Megaspeed has faced allegations that it helped Chinese companies access restricted Nvidia processors, potentially undermining Washington’s export controls.

The controversy intensified following revelations about Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, who previously worked with Megaspeed and was suspected by US intelligence officials of having connections to Beijing.

Also Read | Jensen Huang-Alice Huang affair: How the Nvidia scandal became a US security concern

Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on November 12. However, US authorities have not concluded that Alice Huang was engaged in espionage, and Beijing has rejected the allegations.

Singaporean authorities have separately investigated Megaspeed since February 2025 over possible false declarations relating to server purchases. On Monday, the US Commerce and Justice departments disclosed that Washington had initiated its own investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 over potential export-control violations.

Megaspeed has maintained that it complies with applicable laws, including US export-control requirements.

The episode has also triggered political scrutiny in Washington, with lawmakers questioning whether the administration had done enough to prevent American technology from reaching China.

Fresh evidence raises doubts over the effectiveness of export controls

The restrictions follow research published last week by Unemployment Labs, which found evidence suggesting that several advanced Chinese AI models were developed using Nvidia’s export-restricted Blackwell processors.

The researchers identified numerical fingerprints in models developed by DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group that were consistent with the use of Blackwell hardware.

While the findings do not conclusively establish how or where the chips were accessed, they add to concerns that American export restrictions have not entirely prevented Chinese companies from obtaining advanced computing capabilities.

Separately, research organisation Epoch AI has estimated that around two million advanced AI chips entered China during 2024 and 2025 through arrangements designed to conceal their final destination.

title: Dhoni retires: 5 captaincy masterstrokes that shaped CSK’s title-winning finals
content_html:
Mahendra Singh Dhoni's playing career in the IPL ended on Tuesday after he was appointed the mentor of his franchise Chennai Super Kings. (PTI)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

After 278 matches, 235 of them as captain, 5,439 runs and 24 half-centuries, MS Dhoni has called time on his career as an Indian Premier League (IPL) player. On Tuesday (November 17), Chennai Super Kings announced that their five-time title-winning captain would assume a new role as the team’s mentor.

What defined Dhoni’s tenure at CSK, however, was never merely the runs he accumulated or the sixes he sent soaring into the stands. It was the subtle, delicate decisions not accounted for in the scorecards or statisticians’ notes, but left an indelible mark on the game.

We revisit five such moments — one from each of the five IPL finals in which CSK emerged victorious.

2010: The straight mid-off

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

CSK had come close to a maiden title in each of the first two editions but couldn’t cross the finish line. In 2010, it seemed they finally would, with Mumbai Indians reduced to 114/6 after 17 overs while chasing 168. But Kieron Pollard smashed 22 runs off Doug Bollinger’s next over to drag Mumbai back into the game.

With CSK defending 27 off 7 and Albie Morkel bowling the penultimate over, a fielding tweak from Dhoni earned them their maiden crown. He directed Matthew Hayden at mid-off to go straighter and stand just behind Morkel. Commentating on air, Sunil Gavaskar remarked, “It’s one of the straightest mid-offs you will ever see.” Pollard’s propensity to hit straight proved his undoing, as he was caught at exactly that position.

2011: Ashwin with the new ball

Royal Challengers Bengaluru might not have waited 18 years for a title had it not been for a Dhoni masterclass in the 2011 final. The season belonged to Chris Gayle, who had established himself as T20 cricket’s most destructive batter with 608 runs at a strike rate of 183.13. Gayle had few weaknesses at the time, apart from his vulnerability against off-spin.

Also Read | In Ranchi, parents wanted children to become docs, engineers before Dhoni arrived

Dhoni gave the new ball to Ravichandran Ashwin while defending 205, and on just the fourth delivery of the chase, Gayle fell to an ill-fated cut that took the edge and landed in Dhoni’s gloves.

2018: The backward square leg

Story continues below this ad
Karan Sharma of CSK celebrates after the wicket of Kane Williamson against SRH during the IPL 2018 final against SRH at Wankhede stadium. (Express Photo by Kevin DSouza)

CSK’s seven-year wait for a third title ended in 2018 with an eight-wicket win over Sunrisers Hyderabad. Batting first, SRH were approaching 150 in the 17th over, with captain Kane Williamson having laid the foundation with a 36-ball 47. The onus then fell on Deepak Hooda to provide a strong finish.

Also in Explained | Ball tampering in cricket: The science, history and methods behind it

With Lungi Ngidi bowling, Dhoni placed Dhruv Shorey at backward square leg, and Hooda holed out to him just two deliveries later. Ngidi would go on to acknowledge the role Dhoni’s clever field placements played in CSK’s win.

2021: Thakur’s early return

Chasing 193 in the 2021 final, Kolkata Knight Riders seemed to be cruising towards their third IPL title at 88/0 after 10 overs, with Shubman Gill and Venkatesh Iyer once again working wonders at the top. In the 11th over, Dhoni went back to Shardul Thakur, who had conceded 11 in his first over and would usually be saved for the death. It proved the right call, as Thakur dismissed both Gill and Iyer in that over.

2023: Chahar’s final over

CSK team lift IPL 2023 trophy beating Gujarat Titans at Narendra Modi stadium in Ahmedabad on May 29, 2023. Express photo by Nirmal Harindran, 29-05-2023, Ahmedabad *** Local Caption *** CSK team lift IPL 2023 trophy beating Gujarat Titans at Narendra Modi stadium in Ahmedabad on Monday. (Express photo by Nirmal Harindran)

At 124/1 after 13 overs, Gujarat Titans had exactly the start they wanted in the 2023 final. Even so, Dhoni called on Deepak Chahar to bowl his fourth and final over, despite the seamer having conceded 31 without a wicket in his first three.

Story continues below this ad

It proved to be the downfall of a well-set Wriddhiman Saha, who had already brought up his half-century. Trying to slog a leg-cutter, the keeper edged it to his Chennai counterpart, and the wicket proved crucial given how well Saha was batting.

title: Quad leaders meet in Manila: Why the grouping matters amid Indo-Pacific tensions
content_html:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi poses for a group photo with QUAD Leaders- US President Donald Trump, Japan Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on the sidelines of the ASEAN-India Summit and East Asia Summit, in Manila on Tuesday. (DD/ANI)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

Prime Minister Narendra Modi met US President Donald Trump, Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, and Australian PM Anthony Albanese at the sidelines of the ASEAN Summit for the first meeting in two years of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad) group of Indo-Pacific countries.

This will be Trump’s first Quad leaders’ meeting since beginning his second term in January 2025.

What is the Quad? 

The Quadrilateral Security Dialogue, or Quad, originated as an informal partnership comprising India, Japan, Australia and the US to coordinate disaster relief operations after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

In 2007, Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe proposed a political framework for this grouping.

Right from the outset, the nascent group lacked cohesiveness among its members. Critics argued that they had few strategic aims in common other than an opposition to Chinese territorial assertions in the Indo-Pacific region. China itself accused it of being little more than an anti-China bloc.

After losing its initial momentum, the group was revived nearly a decade later during Trump’s first presidential term in 2017 and broadened its objectives when faced with the rising China challenge.

Why the Quad is not a military alliance like NATO

Unlike a typical multilateral organisation like the United Nations or the European Union, the Quad has no organised physical presence. It does not have a secretariat or a permanent decision-making body.

Story continues below this ad
Also Read | How 2 major summits this week point to balance & bargain strategy in big-power diplomacy

It has, however, focused on expanding existing agreements among member countries and highlighting their shared values.

As an informal grouping, the Quad also lacks provisions for collective defence (unlike NATO’s defining Article 5), relying instead on coordination, strategic dialogue, and joint military exercises to demonstrate alignment.

Questions have also arisen about the Quad’s long-term strategic coherence, particularly as member countries balance economic ties with China alongside security concerns in the Indo-Pacific.

While the Quad was revived during Trump’s first term in 2017, there was ambiguity over its longterm direction given changes in political leadership in member countries and debates over burden-sharing. As a result, India, Japan, and Australia have gained a greater role in sustaining the grouping’s momentum.

Story continues below this ad

What are the Quad’s objectives in the Indo-Pacific?

The grouping took a step towards formalisation in 2020, when the trilateral India-US-Japan Malabar naval exercises expanded to include Australia, marking the first joint military exercises among the four countries in over a decade.

In March 2021, the Quad leaders met virtually amid the Covid pandemic and released a joint statement titled ‘The Spirit of the Quad,’ outlining the group’s approach and objectives.

The first in-person meeting of Quad leaders was also that year in Washington DC.

The Quad’s agenda has since expanded to include resilient supply chains, critical and emerging technologies, cybersecurity, cooperation in semiconductors and critical minerals, and energy security. Recent geopolitical disruptions and the resulting supply chain vulnerabilities have further sharpened the grouping’s focus on economic resilience and strategic coordination.

Story continues below this ad
China This Week | Spotlight on Chinese spying in Jensen Huang saga, and a Xi-Trump-Putin meeting

Given growing tensions in the Indo-Pacific, maritime security remains central to Quad’s outlook, alongside concerns over freedom of navigation and member states’ anxieties about China’s expanding military and maritime presence in the region. The four countries have also coordinated on disaster relief, climate resilience, and health security initiatives.

Quad members have also indicated a willingness to expand the partnership through a so-called Quad Plus that would include South Korea, New Zealand, and Vietnam, amongst others. However, as Major General G G Dwivedi explained in May 2026, Seoul’s focus on the Korean Peninsula and Hanoi’s policy of avoiding military alliances may limit their participation.

title: Blue-chip stocks have performed poorly all year. How did they make a comeback?
content_html:
A view of the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) building in Mumbai which houses Sensex , India's oldest stocks index (Express Photo by Neeraj Priyadarshi)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

Blue-chip stocks, also known as large-caps, have led the market’s rally over the past three weeks, after underperforming for nearly a year. As geopolitical concerns have eased, and other valuation and growth-related concerns have subsided for now, this premium section of the market has emerged as the most attractive risk-reward bet for investors.

Record foreign inflows have followed the recovery in sentiment in November. These have led to a sharp turnaround in the Indian stock market over the past few weeks, outperforming other major global markets.

From being down nearly 15-16% for the year at their lowest in October, the Nifty 50 and Sensex have rallied 11-12% over the last three weeks. Meanwhile, Nifty’s small- and mid-cap indices were up 3-8% in that period.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

“Our view is that things are attractive in the next few quarters from an earnings perspective, and on top of that, valuations were attractive for large-caps. These factors are helping large-caps do better,” said Pankaj Pandey, Head of Research at ICICI Securities.

So, why have blue-chips roared back to life lately after facing persistent issues earlier?

Why blue-chip stocks were performing poorly

Blue-chip companies are well-established and reliable, with massive market capitalisations, known for giving stable and safe returns over a long period of time. Broadly, all companies that are part of the Nifty 50 and Sensex fall under this category.

Mid- and small-caps are the other top 500 companies on the exchange, apart from the blue chips.

Story continues below this ad
Also Read | Stocks down again — but what are the outliers in India’s share market slide?

Since an all-time high in early January, the Nifty 50 had fallen as much as 15% by March. After remaining relatively stable post a brief recovery, it hit its lowest for the year in early October. Despite the recent rally, the index remains 3% below where it ended last year.

On the other hand, the mid- and small-cap indices had been on a roll as investors searched for more attractive bets. Despite undergoing a similar correction to the Nifty 50 and Sensex around March, these indices have soared and remain as much as 6% higher for the year.

In fact, almost all mid- and small-cap indices hit record highs around August and September even as the benchmark indices remained sluggish.

Blue chips turn attractive

The main reason behind mid- and small-caps outperforming blue chips was investors hunting for value deals and higher returns, as a host of problems bogged down the Indian market.

Story continues below this ad

The war in West Asia was the biggest reason, triggering foreign outflows, exorbitant fuel prices, a battering of the rupee, and geopolitical uncertainty.

The focus thus shifted to mid- and small-caps, with the earnings of many of these companies still growing in double digits despite the overall market becoming unattractive, providing the potential of some returns for investors.

However, as things in West Asia have subsided a bit and India has gained from an “anti-AI” sentiment, blue-chip stocks have now overshadowed their counterparts. As the Nifty 50 and Sensex went on a seven-session winning run in early November, reflecting this exuberance, the small- and mid-cap indices were broadly positive but saw ups and downs.

Blue chips have also received strong inflows from foreign investors. Having dumped over $31 billion-worth of shares this year until last month, foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) bought shares worth $9.5 billion in November as of Monday — the highest ever in a month.

Story continues below this ad

The majority of this money has gone into blue chips, which are lower risk compared to the smaller stocks.

“After a prolonged phase of mid- and small-cap outperformance, investors are increasingly shifting towards quality businesses with strong balance sheets, consistent cash flows and reasonable valuations,” explained Mayur Shah, Portfolio Management Services (PMS) Fund Manager at Anand Rathi Advisors.

Earnings revival, valuation comfort

Strong earnings growth reported by blue chips for the July-September quarter and relatively comfortable valuations have turned the “risk-reward ratio” favourable for investors.

Also Read | Why Indians are investing billions abroad amid shaky domestic stock markets

“From a valuation and earnings perspective, large-caps and small-caps are at reasonable valuations, while mid-caps are on the slightly higher side. From this perspective, the large-caps are more attractive in its risk-reward dynamic,” said Pandey of ICICI Securities.

title: Convicted of gangraping pregnant Bilkis Bano, killing family: Why bail now?
content_html:
The Supreme Court on Monday suspended the life sentence of two convicts in the Bilkis Bano case from the 2002 Gujarat riots and granted them bail.

Bano, then aged 21 and five months pregnant, was gang-raped and seven of her family members, including her three-year-old daughter, were killed during the communal riots.

Advertisement

This came over two years after the top court struck down the remission granted to the two, and nine others, by the Gujarat government, and directed them to surrender and return to jail.

What does the latest Supreme Court order say?

Bipinchand Kanaiyalal Joshi and Pradip Ramanlal Modhiya, lodged in a jail in Gujarat, filed a Special Leave to Appeal, challenging the Bombay High Court judgment passed on May 4, 2017, which confirmed their conviction and sentence given by the trial court in 2008.

They told the Supreme Court that they had spent more than 17 years in jail. One of them said that he is severely disabled. The bench of Justice M M Sundresh and Justice Prasanna Varale considered these grounds and said: “Certainly, there are issues to be decided in the appeal, both on fact and law.”

Also Read | Bilkis Bano case: Court records say both convicts were ‘part of mob’, one lived across her house

The court then suspended the sentence and granted bail to the two, directing the trial court to impose terms and conditions. It then directed that their appeals be listed for hearing in due course.

In her response to the Supreme Court’s bail to the two convicts, Bano said she could not believe that the court passed an order “without hearing her”. She said she would fight this order, asking why their sentence was suspended without informing her. According to the law, a victim can be issued a notice and allowed to intervene and make submissions when hearing an appeal.

How were the 11 convicts released the first time around?

To understand this, we must go back to the origins of the legal proceedings. In 2004, the Supreme Court transferred the gang-rape case from Gujarat to Mumbai over apprehensions of evidence tampering and the lack of a conducive situation for a fair trial.

Four years on, a trial court in Mumbai convicted the 11 men of charges including murder, rape and rioting. The convicts appealed this order in the Bombay High Court, which upheld the punishment.

The men then filed Special Leave Petitions before the Supreme Court which, on November 20, 2017, dismissed them, upholding the findings of the High Court as well as the sentence.

The 11 convicts of the Bilkis Bano case were felicitated upon their release from Godhra sub-jail on August 15, 2022. (Express)

In 2022, one of the convicts again approached the top court seeking directions to the Gujarat government for premature release, citing a 1992 remission policy for convicts who had completed at least 14 years in jail. The court asked the Gujarat government to consider the application “within a period of two months”, in line with the policy.

Based on this, a government panel recommended their release and they were released from a Gujarat jail on August 15, 2022. They were felicitated upon their release by local leaders.

Bano filed a petition against their release. Other petitioners, too, approached the court through public interest litigations.

Also Read | ‘I am scared once again’: Bilkis Bano on Supreme Court granting bail to 2 convicts

On January 8, 2024, a Supreme Court division bench said the Gujarat government did not have the authority or jurisdiction to consider the remission applications of the convicts to reduce their sentence as the trial was moved to Mumbai.

This is because such an application can only be taken up by a government within whose territorial jurisdiction the applicant was convicted — in this case, Maharashtra — and not where the offence took place (that is, Gujarat). The court also said that the pleas for remission should have been considered as per a 2014 policy which has a bar for grant of remission to convicts of heinous crimes.

So how was the earlier release different from the current one?

In 2022, the 11 convicts were initially released on remission — which essentially means early release — with their life sentence considered complete. Under Section 432 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), state governments have the power to suspend or remit a sentence.

The criminal justice system has provisions such as remission or reduction of a sentence, taking into account that convicts can reform themselves. But the Supreme Court said in its 2024 order that this has to be balanced with the rights of the victim or her family.

The 11 convicts of the Bilkis Bano case after walking out of the Godhra sub-jail on August 15, 2022. (Express)

The bench said that in prior judgments, the Supreme Court has expressed scepticism over the convict’s claim to a second chance, particularly if the offence is a heinous one. The court also said this is not an indefeasible right.

Unlike remission, the current release is on bail pending appeal. Two of the men, while serving their life sentence, filed a special leave to appeal, challenging their conviction altogether. The division bench was told that they had already spent 17 years in jail, that one of them was implicated nearly three years after the case, and that he was severely disabled.

When the court hears the entire case in detail as part of the appeal, it will go into the specific details on the merits of the case. The bench said that pending the appeal, the two men should be granted bail on grounds including the 17-year incarceration as part of their life sentence. The court also suspended their sentence, which means that their punishment is stayed till the final decision on the appeal. The other convicts can also file separate appeals seeking bail on similar grounds of parity.

According to the law, the court will decide on their pleas, and if it upholds the high court and trial court judgment, and sentences them, they will have to return to jail. The court has said that the appeal will be heard “in its due course”.
